content.title: About
content.content: The cookie, chocolate chip sandwich consists of two soft cookies with a layer of buttery cream in between, topped with chocolate chip pieces. It combines a crisp cookie texture with a smooth, sweet cream and the distinctive aroma of chocolate.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first sandwich‑cookie recipe appeared in the United States in the 1970s.
Original recipes use dark chocolate chips with at least 55 % cocoa content.
The cookies are often packaged in single‑serve packs to keep the cream fresh.
In some markets a pinch of sea salt is added to the cream to enhance flavor.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates from the cookies and fats from the cream provide a quick boost of energy.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Dark chocolate chips are rich in flavonoids, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Calcium from dairy
items.content: The buttery cream, made with milk, contributes to daily calcium intake.

items.title: Milk and gluten allergy
items.content: The product contains wheat flour and dairy ingredients, which may trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The sweet cream and chocolate chips make the snack calorie‑dense; moderate consumption is advised for those monitoring blood sugar.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Some commercial versions use partially hydrogenated oils; choose products labeled trans‑fat free.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the sandwich as a standalone snack, add it to lunch boxes, or crumble it over ice cream or yogurt for a dessert topping.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life keep refrigerated to maintain cream freshness. Discard if the product develops off‑odors or visible mold.

rice-brown-with-soy-based-sauce-fat-adde.title: Brown Rice with Soy‑Based Sauce and Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain product obtained from the whole rice kernel after removing only the outer husk. In this version the rice is cooked with a soy‑based sauce and added fat, which raises its energy value and gives the dish a rich flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ, so it contains more fiber, vitamins, and minerals than white rice.
The soy sauce used is traditionally fermented from soybeans, wheat and salt, providing a characteristic umami taste.
Adding fat (usually a vegetable oil) improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins present in the rice.
Brown rice has a lower glycemic index than white rice, making it more suitable for blood‑sugar control.
In Japan and China rice is often combined with soy sauces in traditional dishes such as “soy‑sauce rice.”

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of magnesium and selenium
items.content: These minerals are important for muscle function, the nervous system and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Beneficial fats and antioxidants in the soy sauce may help lower the risk of heart disease.

items.title: Improved vitamin absorption
items.content: Added fat aids the body in absorbing fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) found in the rice bran.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Brown rice raises blood sugar slowly, which is advantageous for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Soy sauce can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce is salty; people with hypertension should limit portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Added fat increases the calorie count, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: The bran of brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption when consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice as a side dish with vegetables, meat or fish. It can be used in salads, rolls, or as a base for quick stir‑fry meals. When reheating, add a splash of water to prevent drying out.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice with soy sauce should be kept in the refrigerator for no more than 3‑4 days. Reheat to at least 75 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Tiramisu is a classic Italian dessert made of coffee‑soaked ladyfingers, a creamy mixture of mascarpone cheese, eggs, and sugar, and a dusting of cocoa powder. It has a smooth, velvety texture and a distinctive coffee‑chocolate flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tiramisu originated in Venice in the mid‑20th century.
The name “tiramisu” means “pick me up,” referring to the energizing effect of coffee.
The traditional recipe involves no baking; all layers are assembled without heat.
There are many variations, including fruit‑infused, chocolate, and non‑alcoholic versions.
Original recipes use ladyfingers soaked in coffee and sometimes a splash of Marsala wine.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Mascarpone cheese used in the cream is rich in calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Provides protein
items.content: Eggs and mascarpone supply a good amount of protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin A
items.content: Mascarpone provides vitamin A, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Antioxidants from cocoa
items.content: Cocoa powder is high in flavonoids, which may help reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Tiramisu offers quick energy from the carbohydrates in ladyfingers and sugar.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Mascarpone and cream can trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The dessert contains a lot of sugar, which may be problematic for diabetics or those watching their weight.

items.title: Caffeine content
items.content: Coffee‑soaked ladyfingers add caffeine, which can affect sleep and heart rate.

items.title: Raw eggs
items.content: Traditional recipes use raw eggs, posing a risk of salmonella; using pasteurized eggs is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve tiramisu chilled, cut into portions. It can be garnished with extra cocoa, grated chocolate, or fresh berries. For a lighter version, replace part of the cream with yogurt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep tiramisu in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Longer storage may cause the texture and flavor to deteriorate.
